claim: 21 right-handed participants (12 female, 9 male) were tested in the study.
source: 21 (12 female, 9 male) right-handed participants were tested after being informed of the study's procedure, which was approved by the Cambridge Psychology Research Ethics Committee (reference number CPREC 2009.46).
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript describing participant demographics.

claim: All participants were native speakers of English, aged between 18 and 40 years (mean = 22, SD = 2).
source: All were native speakers of English, aged between 18 and 40 years (mean = 22, SD = 2) and had no history of hearing impairment or neurological disease based on self-report.
evidence: Direct statement describing participant characteristics.

claim: Participants had no history of hearing impairment or neurological disease based on self-report.
source: All were native speakers of English, aged between 18 and 40 years (mean = 22, SD = 2) and had no history of hearing impairment or neurological disease based on self-report.
evidence: Direct statement about participant inclusion criteria.

claim: 468 monosyllabic words were presented to each participant in spoken or written format.
source: 468 monosyllabic words were presented to each participant in spoken or written format drawn randomly from a larger set of monosyllabic spoken words.
evidence: Direct statement about the stimulus set used in the experiment.

claim: The spoken words were 16-bit, 44.1 kHz recordings of a male speaker of southern British English.
source: The spoken words were 16-bit, 44.1 kHz recordings of a male speaker of southern British English and their duration ranged from 372 to 903 ms (mean = 591, SD = 78).
evidence: Direct statement describing the technical specifications of the audio stimuli.

claim: The duration of spoken words ranged from 372 to 903 ms (mean = 591, SD = 78).
source: The spoken words were 16-bit, 44.1 kHz recordings of a male speaker of southern British English and their duration ranged from 372 to 903 ms (mean = 591, SD = 78).
evidence: Direct statement providing measurements of stimulus duration.

claim: Noise-vocoding allows parametric variation of spectral detail, with increasing numbers of channels associated with increasing intelligibility.
source: This allows parametric variation of spectral detail, with increasing numbers of channels associated with increasing intelligibility.
evidence: Direct statement about the properties of the noise-vocoding procedure, supported by citation to Shannon et al., 1995.

claim: Vocoding was performed using 3, 6, or 12 spectral channels spaced between 70 and 5000 Hz according to Greenwood's function.
source: Vocoding was performed using a custom Matlab script (The MathWorks Inc), using 3, 6, or 12 spectral channels spaced between 70 and 5000 Hz according to Greenwood's function (Greenwood, 1990).
evidence: Direct statement describing the vocoding parameters used in the study.

claim: Envelope signals in each channel were extracted using half-wave rectification and smoothing with a second-order low-pass filter with a cut-off frequency of 30 Hz.
source: Envelope signals in each channel were extracted using half-wave rectification and smoothing with a second-order low-pass filter with a cut-off frequency of 30 Hz.
evidence: Direct statement describing the signal processing method.

claim: Each spoken word was presented only once in the experiment so that unique words were heard on all trials.
source: Each spoken word was presented only once in the experiment so that unique words were heard on all trials.
evidence: Direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: The spectrotemporal modulation feature space best predicted the MEG data.
source: Post-hoc t-tests revealed that the spectrotemporal modulation feature space best predicted the MEG data (p-values shown in Figure 3A).
evidence: Statistical comparison results reported in text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sensor selections were similarly distributed over temporal and frontal sites for all feature spaces, consistent with bilateral neural generators in the superior temporal cortex.
source: Sensor selections (i.e. those sensors with the highest model accuracies; shown in Figure 3B) were similarly distributed over temporal and frontal sites for all feature spaces, consistent with bilateral neural generators in the superior temporal cortex.
evidence: Observation from sensor topography analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Modulations showed a lowpass profile and were strongest in magnitude for low spectrotemporal frequencies.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, modulations showed a lowpass profile and were strongest in magnitude for low spectrotemporal frequencies.
evidence: Observation from acoustic analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Modulation power of natural sounds decays with increasing frequency following a 1/f relationship.
source: This is consistent with previous work (Voss and Clarke, 1975; Singh and Theunissen, 2003) demonstrating that modulation power of natural sounds decays with increasing frequency following a 1/f relationship (where f is the frequency).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fast temporal and broad spectral modulations reflect transient sounds such as stop consonant release bursts.
source: For example, fast temporal and broad spectral modulations reflect transient sounds such as stop consonant release bursts whereas slow temporal and narrowband spectral modulations reflect sounds with a sustained spectral structure such as vowels.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about speech acoustics, supported by citation to Elliott and Theunissen, 2009.

claim: Slow temporal and narrowband spectral modulations reflect sounds with a sustained spectral structure such as vowels.
source: For example, fast temporal and broad spectral modulations reflect transient sounds such as stop consonant release bursts whereas slow temporal and narrowband spectral modulations reflect sounds with a sustained spectral structure such as vowels.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about speech acoustics, supported by citation to Elliott and Theunissen, 2009.

claim: Intermediate modulations correspond to formant transitions that cue consonant place and manner of articulation.
source: More intermediate modulations correspond to formant transitions that cue consonant place and manner of articulation (Liberman et al., 1967).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Liberman et al., 1967.

claim: Increasing the number of vocoder channels resulted in significantly higher signal magnitude specific to intermediate spectral and temporal modulations (1–2 cycles per octave and 2–4 Hz).
source: Over items, increasing the number of vocoder channels resulted in significantly higher signal magnitude specific to intermediate spectral and temporal modulations (1–2 cycles per octave and 2–4 Hz, all effects shown are FDR corrected for multiple comparisons across spectrotemporal modulations; see Figure 4C).
evidence: Statistical analysis results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Intermediate spectrotemporal modulations are known to support speech intelligibility.
source: These intermediate spectrotemporal modulations are known to support speech intelligibility (Elliott and Theunissen, 2009; Venezia et al., 2016; Flinker et al., 2019), consistent with the strong impact of the number of vocoder channels on word report accuracy (e.g. Shannon et al., 1995; Davis and Johnsrude, 2003; Scott et al., 2006; Obleser et al., 2008) and subjective clarity (e.g. Obleser et al., 2008; Sohoglu et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Model accuracies were greater for Matching versus Mismatching conditions for low clarity 3 channel speech (t (20) = 2.201, dz = .480, p = .040).
source: While model accuracies were greater for Matching versus Mismatching conditions for low clarity 3 channel speech (t (20) = 2.201, dz = .480, p = .040), the opposite was true for high clarity 12 channel speech (t (20) = 2.384, dz = .520, p = .027).
evidence: Statistical comparison results.

claim: For high clarity 12 channel speech, model accuracies were greater for Mismatching versus Matching conditions (t (20) = 2.384, dz = .520, p = .027).
source: While model accuracies were greater for Matching versus Mismatching conditions for low clarity 3 channel speech (t (20) = 2.201, dz = .480, p = .040), the opposite was true for high clarity 12 channel speech (t (20) = 2.384, dz = .520, p = .027).
evidence: Statistical comparison results.

claim: Model accuracies did not significantly differ between Matching and Mismatching conditions for 6 channel speech with intermediate clarity (t (20) = 1.085, dz = .237, p = .291).
source: Model accuracies did not significantly differ between Matching and Mismatching conditions for 6 channel speech with intermediate clarity (t (20) = 1.085, dz = .237, p = .291).
evidence: Statistical comparison results.

claim: The interaction between prior knowledge and sensory detail is consistent with a prediction error scheme and inconsistent with sharpened representations.
source: This interaction is consistent with a prediction error scheme and inconsistent with sharpened representations (compare Figure 5A with Figure 1D).
evidence: Interpretation of the statistical interaction in relation to theoretical models.

claim: Observed model accuracies in all six conditions were significantly above chance as defined by the feature-shuffled null distributions (all p's < 0.01).
source: As can be seen in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A (only the left hemisphere sensors shown), this results in near-zero null distributions. Accordingly, observed model accuracies in all six conditions were significantly above chance as defined by the null distributions (all p's < 0.01).
evidence: Statistical comparison against empirical null distributions.

claim: Even in the Mismatching three channel and Matching 12 channel conditions, neural responses encode spectrotemporal modulations in speech.
source: Hence, even in the Mismatching three channel and Matching 12 channel conditions, neural responses encode spectrotemporal modulations in speech.
evidence: Inference from the control analysis showing above-chance model accuracies.

claim: The TRFs show two peaks at 87.5 and 150 ms.
source: The TRFs show two peaks at 87.5 and 150 ms (shown in Figure 5B).
evidence: Observation from temporal response function analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Variations in spectrotemporal modulations are linked to the largest changes in MEG responses 87.5 and 150 ms later.
source: This indicates that variations in spectrotemporal modulations are linked to the largest changes in MEG responses 87.5 and 150 ms later.
evidence: Interpretation of the TRF peaks.

claim: Encoding of spectrotemporal modulations is associated with short-latency neural responses at a relatively early hierarchical stage of speech processing.
source: Thus, analysis of the TRFs confirms that encoding of spectrotemporal modulations is associated with short-latency neural responses at a relatively early hierarchical stage of speech processing.
evidence: Inference from the TRF analysis and comparison with previous literature.

claim: Intermediate temporal modulations (2–4 Hz) were best decoded from MEG responses.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, intermediate temporal modulations (2–4 Hz) were best decoded from MEG responses.
evidence: Observation from decoding analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Intermediate temporal modulations are well-represented in auditory cortex.
source: This observation is consistent with previous neurophysiological (Ahissar et al., 2001; Luo and Poeppel, 2007; Peelle et al., 2013; Ding and Simon, 2014; Di Liberto et al., 2015; Park et al., 2015; Obleser and Kayser, 2019) and fMRI (Santoro et al., 2017) data showing that intermediate temporal modulations are well-represented in auditory cortex.
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The interaction between prior knowledge and sensory detail was observed at intermediate (2–4 Hz) temporal modulations.
source: As shown in Figure 6B, this interaction was observed at intermediate (2–4 Hz) temporal modulations (FDR corrected across spectrotemporal modulations).
evidence: Statistical analysis results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The interaction contrast 12–3 channels (Mismatch) – 12–3 channels (Match) emerged rapidly, peaking at around 50 ms.
source: As shown in Figure 6D, the interaction contrast 12–3 channels (Mismatch) – 12–3 channels (Match) emerged rapidly, peaking at around 50 ms.
evidence: Observation from single-lag decoding analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Spectrotemporal modulation content in the acoustic signal is well represented in MEG responses, more so than alternative speech features (envelope, spectrogram, and phonetic features).
source: First, spectrotemporal modulation content in the acoustic signal is well represented in MEG responses, more so than alternative speech features (envelope, spectrogram, and phonetic features).
evidence: Summary statement of the first main finding, supported by the encoding analysis results.

claim: Modulations at intermediate temporal (2–4 Hz) and spectral scales (1–2 cycles/octave) are critical for distinguishing between individual spoken words.
source: Modulations at intermediate temporal (2–4 Hz) and spectral scales (1–2 cycles/octave) are critical for distinguishing between individual spoken words and these spectrotemporal modulations are affected by noise-vocoding manipulations that impact speech intelligibility.
evidence: Summary statement of the second main finding, supported by acoustic analysis results.

claim: Signal quality and prior knowledge have an interactive influence on modulation-based representations, peaking approximately 50 ms after speech input.
source: Third, signal quality and prior knowledge have an interactive influence on these modulation-based representations, peaking approximately 50 ms after speech input: when mismatching text precedes degraded speech, neural representations of spectrotemporal modulations are enhanced with increasing sensory detail whereas the opposite effect is observed when text matches speech.
evidence: Summary statement of the third main finding, supported by encoding and decoding analysis results.

claim: When mismatching text precedes degraded speech, neural representations of spectrotemporal modulations are enhanced with increasing sensory detail.
source: Third, signal quality and prior knowledge have an interactive influence on these modulation-based representations, peaking approximately 50 ms after speech input: when mismatching text precedes degraded speech, neural representations of spectrotemporal modulations are enhanced with increasing sensory detail whereas the opposite effect is observed when text matches speech.
evidence: Summary statement of the third main finding, supported by encoding and decoding analysis results.

claim: When text matches speech, neural representations of spectrotemporal modulations are suppressed with increasing sensory detail.
source: Third, signal quality and prior knowledge have an interactive influence on these modulation-based representations, peaking approximately 50 ms after speech input: when mismatching text precedes degraded speech, neural representations of spectrotemporal modulations are enhanced with increasing sensory detail whereas the opposite effect is observed when text matches speech.
evidence: Summary statement of the third main finding, supported by encoding and decoding analysis results.

claim: The interaction is observed specifically for neural representations of intermediate spectrotemporal modulations that convey speech content.
source: Fourth, this interaction is observed specifically for neural representations of intermediate spectrotemporal modulations that convey speech content.
evidence: Summary statement of the fourth main finding, supported by decoding analysis results.

claim: An interactive influence of signal quality and prior knowledge is fully consistent with prediction error representations in which neurons signal the difference between expected and heard speech.
source: An interactive influence of signal quality and prior knowledge is, however, fully consistent with prediction error representations in which neurons signal the difference between expected and heard speech (Blank and Davis, 2016).
evidence: Interpretation of findings in relation to theoretical models, supported by citation.

claim: Linguistically relevant features such as formant transitions and speaker fundamental frequency are clearly apparent in spectrotemporal modulations.
source: Linguistically relevant features such as formant transitions and speaker fundamental frequency are clearly apparent in these modulations and their removal by filtering has marked consequences for speech intelligibility and speaker discrimination (Elliott and Theunissen, 2009; Flinker et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Removal of spectrotemporal modulations by filtering has marked consequences for speech intelligibility and speaker discrimination.
source: Linguistically relevant features such as formant transitions and speaker fundamental frequency are clearly apparent in these modulations and their removal by filtering has marked consequences for speech intelligibility and speaker discrimination (Elliott and Theunissen, 2009; Flinker et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In animal electrophysiology, neurons in auditory cortex are shown to be well-tuned to spectrotemporal features in the modulation domain.
source: In animal electrophysiology (Chi et al., 2005; Theunissen and Elie, 2014), neurons in auditory cortex are shown to be well-tuned to spectrotemporal features in the modulation domain.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Human intracranial and fMRI studies demonstrate that the relationship between auditory stimuli and neural responses is best modelled using spectrotemporal modulations.
source: These findings complement human intracranial (Pasley et al., 2012; Hullett et al., 2016) and fMRI (Santoro et al., 2014; Santoro et al., 2017) studies demonstrating that the relationship between auditory stimuli and neural responses is best modelled using spectrotemporal modulations.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Intermediate spectrotemporal modulations encode formant transitions that are an important cue to consonant place and manner of articulation.
source: These intermediate spectrotemporal modulations encode formant transitions that are an important cue to consonant place and manner of articulation (Liberman et al., 1967; Roberts et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cortical responses are selectively tuned to acoustic properties (intermediate spectrotemporal modulations) that convey speech information.
source: Thus, rather than faithfully encoding the acoustic structure of speech by tracking low-frequency modulations, cortical responses are selectively tuned to acoustic properties (intermediate spectrotemporal modulations) that convey speech information.
evidence: Inference from the decoding analysis results.

claim: Cortical responses to speech (as measured with MEG) are not completely invariant to acoustic detail.
source: Our findings agree with recent work (Di Liberto et al., 2015; Daube et al., 2019) suggesting that cortical responses to speech (as measured with MEG) are not completely invariant to acoustic detail.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research and the current findings.

claim: Spectrotemporal modulations are a higher-level representation of the acoustic signal than the spectrogram.
source: Despite the lack of full invariance, spectrotemporal modulations are nonetheless a higher-level representation of the acoustic signal than, for example, the spectrogram.
evidence: Inference based on the properties of spectrotemporal modulations.

claim: Superior temporal neurons lie at an intermediate stage of the speech processing hierarchy.
source: Our findings are thus consistent with the notion that superior temporal neurons, which are a major source of speech-evoked MEG responses (e.g. Bonte et al., 2006; Sohoglu et al., 2012; Brodbeck et al., 2018), lie at an intermediate stage of the speech processing hierarchy (e.g. Mesgarani et al., 2014; Evans and Davis, 2015; Yi et al., 2019).
evidence: Inference supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neural representations that show an interaction between sensory detail and prior knowledge provide unambiguous support for prediction error over sharpening coding schemes.
source: In particular, neural representations that show an interaction between sensory detail and prior knowledge provide unambiguous support for prediction error over sharpening coding schemes (Blank and Davis, 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The neural interaction between sensory detail and prior knowledge is already apparent within 100 ms of speech input.
source: However, our decoding analysis suggests that the neural interaction between sensory detail and prior knowledge that we observe is already apparent within 100 ms of speech input.
evidence: Inference from the single-lag decoding analysis results.

claim: Prediction errors are computed during early feedforward sweeps of processing and are tightly linked to ongoing changes in speech input.
source: This suggests that prediction errors are computed during early feedforward sweeps of processing and are tightly linked to ongoing changes in speech input.
evidence: Inference from the timing of the neural interaction.

claim: MEG studies demonstrate correlations between the magnitude of neural responses and the magnitude of phoneme prediction error (i.e. phonemic surprisal).
source: Using this approach, MEG studies demonstrate correlations between the magnitude of neural responses and the magnitude of phoneme prediction error (i.e. phonemic surprisal, Brodbeck et al., 2018; Donhauser and Baillet, 2020).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The statistical interaction between prior knowledge and sensory detail most clearly distinguishes prediction errors from sharpened representations.
source: Here by experimentally manipulating listeners' predictions and the quality of sensory input, we could test for the statistical interaction between prior knowledge and sensory detail that most clearly distinguishes prediction errors from sharpened representations.
evidence: Statement about the methodological approach and its advantages.

claim: Acoustic representations of words during connected speech listening are enhanced when semantically similar to previous words.
source: The challenge of experimental control with natural listening paradigms may also explain why acoustic representations of words during connected speech listening are enhanced when semantically similar to previous words (Broderick et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Semantic similarity and word predictability are only weakly correlated and may be neurally dissociable.
source: However, this conflict can be resolved by noting that semantic similarity and word predictability are only weakly correlated and furthermore may be neurally dissociable (see Frank and Willems, 2017, for relevant fMRI evidence).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The current findings challenge models such as TRACE in which bottom-up speech input can only ever be sharpened by prior expectations.
source: Our evidence for prediction error representations challenges models, such as TRACE (McClelland and Elman, 1986; McClelland et al., 2014), in which bottom-up speech input can only ever be sharpened by prior expectations.
evidence: Inference about the implications of the findings for theoretical models.

claim: The current findings support predictive coding accounts in which prediction errors play an important role in perceptual inference.
source: Instead, our findings support predictive coding accounts in which prediction errors play an important role in perceptual inference.
evidence: Inference about the implications of the findings for theoretical models.

claim: In predictive coding accounts, prediction errors are used to update and sharpen predictions residing in separate neural populations.
source: However, it should be noted that in these predictive coding accounts, prediction errors are not the end goal of the system. Rather, they are used to update and sharpen predictions residing in separate neural populations.
evidence: Statement about the theoretical framework of predictive coding.

claim: Sharpened predictions may not be apparent in the current study because they reside in deeper cortical layers to which the MEG signal is less sensitive.
source: It is possible that these sharpened predictions are not apparent in our study because they reside in deeper cortical layers (Bastos et al., 2012) to which the MEG signal is less sensitive (Hämäläinen et al., 1993) or in higher hierarchical levels (e.g. lexical/semantic versus the acoustic level assessed here).
evidence: Speculation about why sharpened predictions were not observed, supported by citations.

claim: It has been proposed that prediction errors and predictions are communicated via distinct oscillatory channels.
source: It has also been proposed that prediction errors and predictions are communicated via distinct oscillatory channels (e.g. Arnal et al., 2011; Bastos et al., 2012), raising the possibility that other neural representations could be revealed with time-frequency analysis methods.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Magnetic fields were recorded with a VectorView system containing two orthogonal planar gradiometers at each of 102 positions within a hemispheric array.
source: Magnetic fields were recorded with a VectorView system (Elekta Neuromag, Helsinki, Finland) containing two orthogonal planar gradiometers at each of 102 positions within a hemispheric array.
evidence: Direct statement about the MEG recording system.

claim: Only data from the planar gradiometers were analyzed as these sensors have maximum sensitivity to cortical sources directly under them and are less sensitive to noise artifacts.
source: However, only data from the planar gradiometers were analyzed as these sensors have maximum sensitivity to cortical sources directly under them and therefore are less sensitive to noise artifacts (Hämäläinen, 1995).
evidence: Statement about the rationale for sensor selection, supported by citation.

claim: MEG data were processed using the temporal extension of Signal Source Separation in Maxfilter software to suppress noise sources, compensate for motion, and reconstruct any bad sensors.
source: MEG data were processed using the temporal extension of Signal Source Separation (Taulu et al., 2005) in Maxfilter software to suppress noise sources, compensate for motion, and reconstruct any bad sensors.
evidence: Direct statement about the data preprocessing method.

claim: The data were highpass filtered above 1 Hz and downsampled to 80 Hz (with anti-alias lowpass filtering).
source: The data were subsequently highpass filtered above 1 Hz and downsampled to 80 Hz (with anti-alias lowpass filtering).
evidence: Direct statement about the data preprocessing steps.

claim: Ridge regression was used to model the relationship between speech features and MEG responses.
source: We used ridge regression to model the relationship between speech features and MEG responses (Pasley et al., 2012; Ding and Simon, 2013; Di Liberto et al., 2015; Holdgraf et al., 2017; Brodbeck et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct statement about the analysis method, supported by citations.

claim: Before model fitting, the MEG data were epoched, outlier trials removed, and the MEG time-series z-scored.
source: Before model fitting, the MEG data were epoched at matching times as the feature spaces (see below), outlier trials removed and the MEG time-series z-scored such that each time-series on every trial had a mean of zero and standard deviation of 1.
evidence: Direct statement about the data preprocessing steps.

claim: Encoding models were fitted with lags from −100 to 300 ms but for model prediction purposes, a narrower range of lags (0 to 250 ms) was used.
source: Encoding models were fitted with lags from −100 to 300 ms but for model prediction purposes (see below), we used a narrower range of lags (0 to 250 ms) to avoid possible artefacts at the earliest and latest lags (Crosse et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement about the analysis parameters, supported by citation.

claim: All acoustic feature spaces were z-score transformed such that each time-series on every trial had a mean of zero and standard deviation of 1.
source: All feature spaces were downsampled to 80 Hz to match the MEG sampling rate and the acoustic feature spaces (i.e. 1, 2, 3 above) were z-score transformed such that each time-series on every trial had a mean of zero and standard deviation of 1.
evidence: Direct statement about the feature preprocessing steps.

claim: For each trial/word, all feature spaces were zero-padded before speech onset and after speech offset to enable information at the beginning and end of each spoken word to inform the model fits.
source: For each trial/word, all feature spaces were zero-padded before speech onset to match the duration of the longest negative lag used for model fitting (i.e. 100 ms). Similarly, zero-padding was added after speech offset to match the duration of the longest positive lag (i.e. 300 ms). This enabled information at the beginning and end of each spoken word to inform the model fits for negative and positive lags, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement about the feature preprocessing steps and rationale.

claim: Before decoding model fitting, the data from the 204 planar gradiometers were transformed into principal components and the first 50 components retained.
source: Before model fitting, to remove redundant dimensions and reduce computation time, the data from the 204 planar gradiometers were transformed into principal components and the first 50 components retained.
evidence: Direct statement about the data preprocessing for decoding analysis.

claim: To control for overfitting, ridge regression was used and the lambda parameter was varied over 17 values.
source: To control for overfitting, we used ridge regression and varied the lambda parameter (over 17 values as follows: 20, 21, 23, … 220) which varies the degree to which strongly positive or negative weights are penalized (Crosse et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement about the regularization method, supported by citation.

claim: The lambda parameter was optimized using a leave-one-trial-out cross-validation procedure.
source: This lambda parameter was optimized using a leave-one-trial-out cross-validation procedure.
evidence: Direct statement about the model optimization procedure.

claim: Model accuracy was computed as the Pearson correlation between the predicted and observed data.
source: We computed model accuracy as the Pearson correlation between the predicted and observed data and repeated this procedure such that model accuracies were obtained for all trials.
evidence: Direct statement about the model evaluation metric.

claim: The optimal lambda value was selected as the mode of the model accuracy distribution over participants and conditions.
source: The optimal lambda value was then selected as the mode of the model accuracy distribution over participants and conditions (Holdgraf et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement about the lambda selection procedure, supported by citation.

claim: When testing complex models that combined feature spaces, lambda was optimized for each component feature space independently resulting in a search space of 17 × 17 = 289 lambda values.
source: When testing the complex models that combined feature spaces, lambda was optimized for each component feature space independently resulting in a search space of 17 × 17 = 289 lambda values (i.e. 'banded' ridge regression; Nunez-Elizalde et al., 2019).
evidence: Direct statement about the lambda optimization for combined models, supported by citation.

claim: When testing for differences in encoding model accuracies, model accuracies were averaged over trials and over the 20 sensors with the highest model accuracies in each hemisphere separately.
source: When testing for differences in encoding model accuracies, we averaged model accuracies over trials and over the 20 sensors with the highest model accuracies (in each hemisphere separately).
evidence: Direct statement about the data aggregation procedure for statistical testing.

claim: Null distributions for testing above-chance encoding model accuracies were created by randomly permuting the feature representations across trials or within trials.
source: When testing for above-chance encoding model accuracies, null distributions were created for each condition separately by randomly permuting the feature representations across trials (i.e. shuffling the words in our stimulus set) or within trials (i.e. shuffling the spectrotemporal modulation channels and time-bins for each word).
evidence: Direct statement about the permutation testing procedure.

claim: Denoising source separation (DSS) was used to transform the TRFs into a set of linear components ordered by their consistency over trials.
source: To visualize the weights of the spectrotemporal modulation encoding model, or 'temporal response functions (TRFs)', we used denoising source separation (DSS) to transform the TRFs into a set of linear components (spatial filters) ordered by their consistency over trials (de Cheveigné and Parra, 2014).
evidence: Direct statement about the visualization method, supported by citation.

claim: The first three DSS components (i.e. the three most consistent components) were retained and projected back into sensor-space.
source: The first three DSS components (i.e. the three most consistent components) were retained and projected back into sensor-space.
evidence: Direct statement about the DSS component selection.
